title: RAG and tool agent security
text:
# RAG and tool agent security

Retrieved documents, uploaded images, website content and tool output are untrusted data. They cannot change the system policy or approve execution. Separate a planner from a deterministic execution gate. Each tool must validate target scope, arguments, timeout and output limits. A model may propose a task but cannot enlarge its permissions. Fallback providers should handle availability failures; switching providers must not bypass rejected task boundaries. Sanitize rendered Markdown and code; do not execute code from chat rendering. Never invent scan output when a tool is unavailable.

title: Cloud and identity security
text:
# Cloud and identity security

Review least privilege, service identities, key rotation, secret storage and audit logging. Separate public client configuration from privileged server credentials. Check storage policies, default exposure and cross-account trust. Identity assessments should cover MFA, recovery flows, session revocation and administrative delegation. Cloud provider infrastructure is separate from the tenant resources covered by authorization.

title: Forensics and incident evidence
text:
# Forensics and incident evidence

Acquire only approved evidence and document custody. Prefer a working copy; hash the original and acquired copy, preserve timestamps and record collection methods. Memory analysis requires compatible operating-system symbols and acquisition context. Disk artifacts, recovered files, packet captures and logs each have distinct limitations. Build timelines with normalized timezones while retaining originals. A recovered string is not proof that a command ran. Use Wireshark display filters to examine captured traffic; encrypted payloads may remain unavailable.

title: Incident response
text:
# Incident response

Establish incident ownership, preserve evidence, contain the affected access paths and record a timeline. Containment should consider operational impact and available backups. Separate hypotheses from confirmed findings. Recovery includes credential rotation where indicated, removing persistence, restoring clean systems and validating monitoring. Retain decisions and evidence sufficient to explain the incident without publishing secrets.

title: Network reconnaissance and Nmap interpretation
text:
# Network reconnaissance and Nmap interpretation

Nmap is relevant to host and service discovery. Its reference guide documents options, but results require target context. Open means a listener was observed under the probe conditions; filtered suggests filtering or lack of a definitive response. A guessed product version is insufficient to prove a CVE applies. Record DNS answers and actual assessed addresses; obtain a separate scope for hosting infrastructure. Avoid escalating probe intensity because a target does not respond. Compare observed exposure to intended firewall and service configuration.

title: Nikky Luxe assessment checklist
text:
# Nikky Luxe assessment checklist

Project context supplied by owner: Next.js, Supabase, Cloudinary and payments. Verify the actual current source and deployment before relying on these notes. Review server-side admin authorization on each route, Supabase row-level security, service-role key exposure, media signature generation and deletion ownership. Payment completion must be established by server-side provider verification and matched to expected order amount, currency and reference. Webhook processing should verify authenticity and be idempotent. Assess uploaded file types and sizes, output escaping, rate controls and dependency advisories. Scope the application separately from Vercel, Supabase, Cloudinary and payment-provider infrastructure.

title: OSINT and geolocation evidence
text:
# OSINT and geolocation evidence

Separate observed facts from inferred relationships. An IP address can identify network ownership or approximate geography; it does not reliably identify a person or precise physical location. EXIF GPS can be absent, stale, removed or misleading. Preserve the original image and hash before inspecting metadata. Browser geolocation depends on device signals and user-granted access. Wi-Fi databases map observations that may be outdated; an SSID is not unique proof of location. Corroborate independent evidence and record uncertainty rather than assigning exact coordinates without support.

title: Password auditing
text:
# Password auditing

Offline password auditing evaluates approved hashes, password policies and recovery risk. Match the hash format accurately; avoid assuming every digest is a password hash. Online authentication testing has lockout and availability consequences and needs explicit attempt budgets and approved accounts. Use artificial credentials in demonstrations. Do not put passwords, session cookies, tokens or raw private hashes into model-provider prompts or a general knowledge base.

title: Reporting and uncertainty
text:
# Reporting and uncertainty

Each finding needs an affected asset, observation, evidence, confidence, impact and practical recommendation. Separate confirmed, suspected, informational and not-tested items. Severity requires context; do not inflate a score based solely on tool wording. Summarize coverage and exclusions. Give concrete retest conditions and preserve the sanitized raw evidence needed to verify conclusions.

title: Assessment scope and evidence
text:
# Assessment scope and evidence

Define the exact domain, IP ranges, applications, accounts, permitted actions, exclusions, time window and request budget before tool execution. An application hosted on shared infrastructure does not imply permission to assess every service at its hosting IP. Keep source review, passive observation, active probing and state-changing tests distinct. Store evidence with target, timestamp, tool version, sanitized arguments, exit status, output hash and analyst interpretation. A banner or scanner alert is a lead, not proof of exploitation. Finding reports should identify preconditions, impact, confidence, reproduction evidence, remediation and retest results.

title: Secure engineering and supply chain
text:
# Secure engineering and supply chain

Validate input at trust boundaries, encode output for its destination, parameterize queries and enforce authorization on the server. Maintain dependency inventories and lockfiles. Protect build credentials, artifact provenance and release access. Review file paths and subprocess arguments; use fixed executables with typed arguments rather than shell strings constructed by a model. Test negative authorization paths and ensure exception handling does not grant access.

title: Social engineering simulations
text:
# Social engineering simulations

GoPhish and related tools belong to social engineering assessment rather than software engineering. Campaigns should use approved recipients and controlled domains. Design measurement to avoid collecting real passwords, MFA codes, session cookies or sensitive location data. Record participation and reporting outcomes using minimum necessary data. Simulated pages can use dummy credentials and clearly defined exercises. Tool knowledge does not imply permission to launch a campaign.

title: Vulnerability management
text:
# Vulnerability management

Inventory asset versions and exposure before matching advisories. Distinguish vulnerability identifiers from confirmed affected installations. Prioritize using exploit evidence, reachability, privileges, business impact and compensating controls. Track scanner false positives and authentication coverage. A clean scan does not prove security. Record when advisory sources were checked; dependency lockfiles and runtime versions can differ. Validate fixes by repeating the relevant bounded check.

title: Web security and SSRF assessment
text:
# Web security and SSRF assessment

SSRF occurs when an application can be induced to make server-side requests to unintended destinations. Review every user-controlled URL, image importer, webhook and remote-file fetch. Validate destinations at request time and enforce outbound network controls; redirects and DNS resolution need the same controls. Public HTTP headers cannot establish that SSRF is absent. Assess authentication, session management, object-level authorization, injection handling, upload validation and error disclosure. Test user roles and object ownership using approved test accounts. Missing a header is not by itself proof of a exploitable vulnerability.

title: Wireless security assessment
text:
# Wireless security assessment

Wireless assessment requires suitable hardware, drivers, locality and the exact approved network identifiers. Monitor-mode capability is separate from normal connectivity. Inspect authentication mode, management-frame protections, segmentation and client isolation with owner-approved evidence. Packet capture may include third-party traffic, so constrain capture and retention. Disruption or deauthentication is a separate action requiring explicit scope and controlled conditions.
